messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kahu's Case

Kahu was fifty-six years old when he first sat down in the therapist's office, his broad shoulders hunched forward, his hands clasped so tightly that the knuckles had gone pale. He was a detective with the Honolulu Police Department—had been for twenty-eight years—and he had come because his ex-wife had finally stopped answering his calls, his captain had pulled him off active cases pending a fitness evaluation, and he could no longer remember the last time he had slept through a single night. What Kahu did not say in that first session, but what emerged over the following weeks, was that he had spent the last three decades running from a boy who no longer existed, and that boy was catching up.

Kahu had grown up in Kailua with his grandmother after his mother's death. His grandmother's partner, a man named Frank, had moved in when Kahu was seven. Frank was a large man with a temper that seemed to ignite without warning, and he had particular fury for the smell of burnt food—a smell that meant carelessness, disrespect, laziness. When Kahu was nine, he had left a pot on the stove too long. The smell filled the small house. Frank had beaten him across the kitchen and into the hallway, and that smell—acrid, choking, unmistakable—had become fused in Kahu's nervous system with the certainty of pain. The beatings continued sporadically over the next nine years, always worse when Frank had been drinking, always accompanied by his voice saying Kahu was worthless, that he deserved it, that he was the kind of boy who made men angry.

Kahu had become a detective because he needed to be the one in control, the one watching, the one who saw danger before it arrived. For decades, this had worked. He was good at his job—methodical, observant, relentless. But in the last five years, the compartments had begun to fail. He had started avoiding wearing the blue polo shirts that reminded him, in some way he could not quite articulate, of the kind of shirt Frank had worn. He had stopped going to the precinct gym because a younger officer there had similar dark hair and a similar build, and Kahu found himself unable to be in the same room without his chest tightening, his mind fragmenting into something that was no longer quite present. He had begun taking solo shifts, turning down invitations to the weekly poker games, eating lunch alone in his car.

The worst trigger was the burnt smell. Three months ago, a house fire had been ruled arson, and Kahu had been assigned to the case. He had walked into that charred kitchen and the smell had hit him like a physical blow—not metaphorically, but literally: his legs had nearly buckled, his vision had narrowed, and for several minutes he had been nine years old again, waiting for the next blow to fall. He had finished the investigation, but something had shifted. Now, whenever he smelled anything burnt—a colleague's overcooked lunch, a neighbor's barbecue—his body would flood with adrenaline, his heart would race, and he would find himself scanning the room for exits, for threats, for the man who was no longer there.

What frightened Kahu most was not the memories themselves, though they came without warning and with a rage that terrified him. It was the moments when he felt something other than rage—a laugh with a colleague, a warm afternoon, the simple peace of finishing a good meal—because in those moments, he was certain that something terrible was about to happen. He had come to believe that contentment was a setup, that his own capacity to feel okay was a character flaw, a sign of weakness that the universe would punish. He was, he was certain, a lousy coper. The fact that he had survived, that he had built a career and a life, only proved to him that he was fundamentally broken in ways he could not quite explain.

When he tried to talk about what had happened, the narrative would dissolve. He would begin to describe Frank, the kitchen, the smell, and then something would scatter inside him and he would lose the thread entirely, left sitting in silence, ashamed. His ex-wife had finally told him that she could not be married to someone who was not present, who could not explain what was happening inside him, who seemed to be disappearing further every year. She had not said it unkindly. She had just said it was true.

Now, at fifty-six, Kahu was sleeping perhaps three hours a night, his body refusing to fully rest because some part of him still needed to stay alert, to watch, to be ready. He had requested the intake appointment because his captain had made it clear that his job depended on it. But what Kahu was truly hoping for, though he could barely admit it to himself, was the possibility that he might finally understand why a boy who had done nothing wrong had come to believe that he deserved what happened, and whether it was possible to stop running long enough to actually live.
